summary:
Rule for the last two weeks: set the agenda on issues the change bloc owns or can take over, contest Netanyahu's record on accountability and competence rather than identity, and use right-coded messengers for soft Netanyahu-bloc voters. Do not give Likud the identity fight it wants.

Agenda and ownership. News attention changes which problems voters weigh (D8-F01). Some of that is voters learning party positions and adopting their own side's view (D8-F02). Ads on owned issues work better than ads on a rival's issues (D8-F03). Ownership pays only among voters who rate the issue as important (D8-F04). Ownership can move, mostly on unowned issues (D8-F05). Reframing an issue and blaming the rival's record cut that rival's ownership by about 7 points (0.25 SD). Copying its position did not work (D8-F06). A military biography raises perceived security competence regardless of party, but not warmth (D8-F07). That is Eisenkot's route: security as competence and accountability, not hawkishness. Israeli precedent is sobering. Cost of living led the agenda in 2013 and 2015, but ownership of it was split while Netanyahu held the security lead (53% vs 14%; 39% vs 22%), and he won (D8-F08). In 2022 ex-chiefs of staff gained little, because voters read security through identity and national narrative (D8-F09, D8-F10).

2026 data. Among Jews the first-ranked vote factor is spread out: security 18%, economy 18%, leader 16%, conscription 14%, religion-state 13%, judicial 6% (D8-F12). Right-wing Jews rank cost of living first, and 43% say voting changes nothing (D8-F13). The draft is the cross-bloc wedge: 71.5% of Jews oppose the freeze on arresting yeshiva draft evaders. The judicial and AG laws split by camp (D8-F14). The Netanyahu bloc's best wedge is Arab parties in a coalition, which 59-61% oppose (D8-F15). October 7 accountability has become partisan. In 2023, 69% of Likud voters wanted Netanyahu to take responsibility. Now 27% of coalition voters say he bears 'a great deal' of it, while 37-52% back a state commission (D8-F16). Satisfaction with the IDF runs 27 points above satisfaction with the government (D8-F17). Israeli security crises produce hawkishness and trust in the army, not a rally behind a government whose responsibility is contested (D8-F11).

Negativity and emotion. Attacks barely hurt targets, bring backlash on the attacker, and do not depress turnout on average (D8-F18). They demobilise only voters already committed to the attacked candidate (D8-F19). In multi-candidate races the bystander gains 3.7 pp (D8-F20). Out-group language raises the odds of sharing by 67% per term (D8-F21). Anger mobilises (D8-F23). Threats to a party's status enrage its strong identifiers (D8-F24). Triumphalism therefore risks waking up Likud's base. Fear and loss frames persuade (d = 0.29), especially when paired with an action (D8-F25). Enthusiasm mobilises your own side (D8-F22).

Reframing, messengers, testing. A loyalty-framed critique cut conservatives' likelihood of voting for Trump by about 19 of 100 points. Pooled behavioural effects are small (d = 0.22) (D8-F26, D8-F27). Out-party leaders polarise (D8-F28). Military elites and in-group critics who pay a price for speaking are credible (D8-F29). Coded religious language reaches religious voters (D8-F30). Shared-identity appeals reduce animosity (D8-F31). Testing pays: targeting on one trait yields up to +70%, video adds little over text, and strong frames beat repeated ones (D8-F32, P-F05). Inoculation works but fades after about two weeks, so the 'Arab-backed government' attack should be pre-empted now (D8-F33). High-turnout messages beat 'gevalt' alarms (D8-F34). Poll momentum creates bandwagons (D8-F35).

Implications:
- What to say: security competence and accountability (a commission, not personal guilt), equal burden, and cost of living.
- Who says it to soft-right and traditional voters: Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, ex-security chiefs and religious figures, not Golan or Lapid.
- What to avoid outside the base: leading on judicial reform, contempt for Haredim or Likud voters, triumphalism, and anything that makes Arab-party partnership salient.

Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out. No Israeli experiment on messengers or reframing was found.

findings.topic: Agenda-setting and priming (experimental)
findings.claim: In two controlled experiments, television news decided which national problems viewers rated as important. The problems that led the news then carried more weight when viewers judged the president's performance. This is the foundational causal evidence that campaigns and media can change the criteria voters use, not only the information they hold. Iyengar & Kinder's book 'News That Matters' (1987) extended it into a full research programme.
findings.quant: Experimental (lab) designs. The abstract reports the effects as qualitative ('profoundly affect'). No pooled effect size.
findings.authors: Shanto Iyengar; Mark D. Peters; Donald R. Kinder
findings.title: Experimental Demonstrations of the 'Not-So-Minimal' Consequences of Television News Programs
findings.relevance: This is why salience is the main lever. With almost no cross-bloc switchers (D5-F08), the bloc gains most by raising the weight Netanyahu-bloc voters give to issues where Netanyahu is weak: the draft, October 7 accountability and cost of living. The Israeli replication is Sheafer & Weimann (P-F32).

findings.topic: Priming is often learning, not re-weighting
findings.claim: A re-analysis of four classic priming cases with panel data found little real priming. Campaign attention to an issue mainly teaches some voters where the parties stand, and they then adopt their own preferred party's position. Salience alone therefore does not automatically turn an issue against the incumbent. Partisans may instead realign their issue views to match their side.
findings.quant: Four cases re-analysed with panel data: 'little evidence of priming effects'.
findings.authors: Gabriel S. Lenz
findings.title: Learning and Opinion Change, Not Priming: Reconsidering the Priming Hypothesis
findings.relevance: Prime issues on which Netanyahu-bloc voters already disagree with their own government, such as the draft (D8-F14). On issues where they follow their camp, such as judicial reform (D1-F06), salience campaigns may simply harden partisan positions.

findings.topic: Issue ownership: theory and ad experiments
findings.claim: Petrocik's theory holds that parties have reputations for handling particular problems. Campaigns win by making the election about issues they 'own'. Petrocik illustrates the theory with the 1980 US election. Experimental tests by Ansolabehere & Iyengar found candidates gain most from advertising on issues they can claim to own. Timing ads to match the news ('riding the wave') added nothing.
findings.quant: Ansolabehere & Iyengar: two experimental studies; ownership hypothesis supported, no interaction between advertising and news.
findings.authors: John R. Petrocik | Stephen Ansolabehere & Shanto Iyengar
findings.title: Issue Ownership in Presidential Elections, with a 1980 Case Study | Riding the Wave and Claiming Ownership Over Issues: The Joint Effects of Advertising and News Coverage in Campaigns
findings.venue: American Journal of Political Science 40(3):825-850 | Public Opinion Quarterly 58(3):335
findings.relevance: Each change-bloc list should advertise on the issue it owns: Yashar on security competence, Together and YB on the draft and equal burden, Together on the economy, Democrats on democracy and religion-state for the base. Ads that echo the day's news, for example on Likud's security agenda, are not themselves a reason to spend.

findings.topic: Ownership matters only when the issue is salient to the voter
findings.claim: Using individual-level data from the 1997 and 2000 Canadian federal elections, the authors show that seeing a party as best on an issue predicts the vote only among voters who consider that issue important. Ownership without salience is electorally inert, and salience without ownership helps the owner.
findings.quant: Conditional (interaction) effect. No single pooled coefficient reported here.
findings.authors: Éric Bélanger; Bonnie M. Meguid
findings.title: Issue salience, issue ownership, and issue-based vote choice
findings.relevance: Making security salient helps the change bloc only where Eisenkot is seen as more competent than Netanyahu. Otherwise it helps Likud. The bloc should pair security salience with a competence or accountability comparison and target the issue to voters who already rank it first (D8-F12).

findings.topic: Issue ownership can be shifted by media performance
findings.claim: In a Belgian online experiment with about 5,000 subjects, a fake TV news item showed the five main party leaders stating their parties' positions on six issues. Exposure significantly shifted which party respondents saw as owning each issue. Shifts were largest on issues no party owned. On issues a party already owned, the effect depended on how balanced the news item was.
findings.quant: N about 5,000; six issues; significant shifts after one exposure.
findings.authors: Stefaan Walgrave; Jonas Lefevere; Michiel Nuytemans
findings.title: Issue Ownership Stability and Change: How Political Parties Claim and Maintain Issues Through Media Appearances
findings.relevance: Issues that no party clearly owns in 2026 are the best ground to claim in two weeks. These include the draft and equal burden, the October 7 commission, and northern recovery. Leader-delivered performances in news formats, such as debates and interviews, are the vehicle.

findings.topic: Issue-ownership attack: reframe and blame, do not copy
findings.claim: Survey experiments in Denmark (agriculture) and the US (business, climate) tested three ways for a party to erode a rival's issue ownership. Reframing the issue in its own terms and blaming the rival for poor performance both cut the rival's ownership score. Moving toward the rival's position did not, and could backfire with the attacker's own voters. Seeberg cites earlier case studies where taking over a rival's issue had large electoral consequences, for example Clinton on crime (Holian 2004).
findings.quant: Reframing lowered the target party's ownership by about 7 points on a 0-1 scale (about 0.25 SD; SD = 0.29-0.32). Blame was 'similarly consistent and a little stronger'. Position accommodation had no effect on 2 of 3 issues.
findings.authors: Henrik Bech Seeberg
findings.title: Issue ownership attack: how a political party can counteract a rival's issue ownership
findings.relevance: This is the evidence for Yashar's security strategy. Reframe security from toughness to competence and accountability ('who prevented the commission, who failed on October 7'), and do not out-hawk Likud. A 7-point dent matters only where security ratings of the two leaders are close.

findings.topic: Military background raises perceived security competence
findings.claim: In an experiment using real campaign ads and handbills with the party label varied, a military-service cue markedly raised ratings of the candidate's ability to handle defence and security, whichever party the candidate belonged to. It did not improve perceived leadership or warmth toward the candidate.
findings.quant: Security-competence ratings 'markedly higher' with the military cue regardless of party. No effect on leadership or affect.
findings.authors: Jeremy M. Teigen
findings.title: Military Experience in Elections and Perceptions of Issue Competence
findings.relevance: Eisenkot's and Abu Rokon's (D6-F21) biographies are an issue-competence asset on security. They are not a likeability asset. Use them in security-competence comparisons, and do not expect them to warm voters to Yashar on other issues.

findings.topic: Israeli ownership precedents: security vs cost of living (2013, 2015)
findings.claim: Before the 2013 election, Israeli Jews rated Netanyahu most suitable on political-security issues and Labor's Yachimovich most suitable on socio-economic issues. In January 2015 a majority named social issues and cost of living as their top concern. Netanyahu still led on security, and ownership of cost of living was split among Kahlon, Herzog, Bennett and Lapid. Netanyahu won both elections. The 2015 late gains came from within his own bloc (D1-F08).
findings.quant: IDI, 31 Dec 2012-2 Jan 2013 (Jews), security: Netanyahu 53%, Yachimovich 14%, Liberman 28%, Bennett 25%; socio-economic: Yachimovich 45%, Netanyahu 36%, Lapid 25%. Channel 10/Midgam, Jan 2015: top issue cost of living and social 53%, security 24%; best on security Netanyahu 39%, Herzog 22%; best on social Kahlon 31%, Herzog 21%, Netanyahu 10%.
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute (Peace Index) | Marissa Newman (Times of Israel), reporting Channel 10/Midgam
findings.title: Israelis Find Netanyahu Most Suitable to Handle Security, Yachimovich for Socio-Economic Issues | Cost of living tops list of election issues - poll
findings.venue: Israel Democracy Institute | The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: A salient economic agenda did not beat Netanyahu when the opposition split ownership of it and he kept the security lead. In 2026 the bloc needs one clear owner per issue and a contest on security itself, not a pivot away from it.

findings.topic: Security credentials now filtered through identity (2022 analysis)
findings.claim: Before the 2022 election, two Israeli political scientists argued that security no longer decides Israeli votes as it once did. Lavi (Bar-Ilan) said election surveys show the democracy and Netanyahu axis dominating since 2019. Rahat (Hebrew University/IDI) said voters first choose a person or ideology and then credit that choice with providing security. Security is now symbolised by Ben Gvir and Smotrich, who had no senior command. On this view, National Unity's former chiefs of staff (Gantz, Eisenkot) gained little from their credentials.
findings.quant: No new data. Expert interpretation of INES trends. National Unity won 12 seats in 2022.
findings.authors: Debbie Mohnblatt (The Media Line), quoting Liron Lavi and Gideon Rahat
findings.title: Being security expert no longer key to winning Israeli elections
findings.relevance: A caution on D8-F07: credentials raise perceived competence but do not override identity. Security messaging must reach voters through in-group identity, as a patriotic, mamlachti (statist), Jewish narrative (D8-F10), not as expert authority alone.

findings.topic: Narrative proximity predicts Israeli vote choice
findings.claim: The authors coded the national stories told in Knesset speeches and measured voters' agreement with fundamental Israeli national narratives in the 2009 election. Holding demographics and ideology constant, voters were significantly more likely to choose parties whose national story matched their own, for most parties.
findings.quant: 2009 Knesset election. Logistic regressions with controls. Narrative-proximity effect significant for most parties.
findings.authors: Tamir Sheafer; Shaul R. Shenhav; Kenneth Goldstein
findings.title: Voting for Our Story: A Narrative Model of Electoral Choice in Multiparty Systems
findings.relevance: For soft-right and traditional voters, frame accountability, equal burden and security in the shared Zionist story of sacrifice, responsibility and mamlachtiut. Liberal-universalist or anti-religious framings mismatch these voters' narrative and lose them.

findings.topic: Security threat in Israel: rally behind the army, not the government
findings.claim: A panel of 939 Jewish Israelis, interviewed before and after October 7, found strong support for the war and trust in the security forces. Trust in the government and the prime minister stayed low. Support for the war tracked threat perceptions and anger at the enemy. Trust in Netanyahu tracked whether respondents blamed the government or the protest movement, and that blame was rooted in their prior views of judicial reform. In the less polarised 2014 Gaza war, by contrast, ethno-national identification did produce a rally behind Netanyahu (Feinstein 2018). A separate Israeli-Palestinian panel shows personal exposure to violence raises distress and threat perceptions, and through them militancy (Hirsch-Hoefler et al. 2016).
findings.quant: Feinstein & Ben-David: n = 939, waves Mar-Apr 2023, Oct 2023, Dec 2023. Hirsch-Hoefler et al.: Israelis n = 996, Palestinians n = 631.
findings.authors: Yuval Feinstein & Geffen Ben-David | Yuval Feinstein | Sivan Hirsch-Hoefler, Daphna Canetti, Carmit Rapaport & Stevan E. Hobfoll
findings.title: United or Divided? A Polarized Society's Response to War | One flag, two rallies: Mechanisms of public opinion in Israel during the 2014 Gaza war | Conflict will Harden your Heart: Exposure to Violence, Psychological Distress, and Peace Barriers in Israel and Palestine
findings.venue: Public Opinion Quarterly 90(3):657-696 | Social Science Research 69:65-82 | British Journal of Political Science 46(4):845-859
findings.relevance: If a security flare-up happens before 27 Oct, threat will push attitudes hawkish (D1-F30, D1-F31). It need not produce a rally to Netanyahu while his responsibility is contested. Eisenkot should stand with the IDF and keep the responsibility frame, and avoid any message that reads as blaming the army or 'the protesters'.

findings.topic: 2026: first-ranked vote factor and doubts about security operations' motives
findings.claim: IDI's August 2026 survey asked for the single factor with the greatest influence on the vote. This complements the top-2 shares in D5-F21. Among Jews no issue dominates. The same survey asked about Israel's strike in Syria near the Turkish border. Half of Jews saw it as mainly defensive. About three in ten saw it as mainly driven by the government's election considerations.
findings.quant: Jews, first factor: security 18.3%, economy and cost of living 17.9%, party head 15.5%, conscription 13.7%, religion-state 13.4%, judicial reform 6.4%. Second factor: security 21.7%, economy 21.2%, conscription 14.2%. Arabs, first factor: crime 31.5%, economy 18.9%. Syria strike: mainly defence 49.4% of Jews, mainly election politics 29.6%, don't know 21.0% (Arabs 57.0% politics). Fieldwork 31 Aug-3 Sep 2026; n = 605 Hebrew + 150 Arabic; ±3.57%.
findings.authors: Viterbi Family Center, Israel Democracy Institute
findings.title: The Israeli Voice Index - August 2026 (data tables)
findings.relevance: With no dominant issue, the bloc's gains come from matching the issue to the segment (D5-F21), not from one national theme. A sizeable minority already suspects electoral motives behind security operations. The bloc should not make that accusation itself, which would look unpatriotic, but it limits how far a late operation can reset the agenda in Likud's favour.

findings.topic: Issues by camp and right-wing political efficacy (IDI Democracy Index 2025)
findings.claim: IDI's pre-election review of its 2025 Democracy Index found that the issue with the greatest impact differs by camp. Right-wing Jews put cost of living first, then October 7. Centrists put the hostages and the Haredi conscription legislation first. The left put the hostages and judicial reform first. Right-wing Jews were also far more likely than left-wing Jews to say it makes no difference who you vote for. Only 26% said any party closely represents them, the lowest since 2003.
findings.quant: 'Makes no difference who you vote for': agree Left 15%, Centre 36%, Right 43% (Jews); total 40% agree, 56% disagree. Jews' issues with greatest impact: hostages, October 7, Haredi conscription, cost of living and judicial reform each 16-18%. Closely represented by a party: 26%.
findings.authors: Viterbi Family Center, Israel Democracy Institute
findings.title: Special Review of Public Opinion Ahead of 2026 Elections (IDI's Israeli Democracy Index)
findings.relevance: Cost of living is the one bloc message that reaches the right's own top concern. Low efficacy on the right means soft Netanyahu-bloc voters can drift to abstention. Do not attack them in ways that energise them (D8-F24). Pre-war data, so treat the camp ranking as indicative.

findings.topic: The draft unites, the judicial agenda divides (IDI July 2026)
findings.claim: Shortly after the Knesset dissolved, IDI asked about three laws it had passed. About seven in ten Jews opposed the law freezing arrests of yeshiva students who do not report for service. Majorities also opposed the attorney-general law and the gender-segregation law, but these split by camp. Right-wing support for the arrest freeze was lower than its support for the AG law, while a small right-wing majority backed the AG law. Among Jewish religiosity groups, only Haredim showed very high support for the arrest freeze.
findings.quant: Jews: arrest freeze 25.3% support, 71.5% oppose (57.2% strongly); AG law 35.5% support, 52.3% oppose; gender segregation 31.0% support, 64.8% oppose. Left support for each law 5-6%, centre 14-18%. Fieldwork 28 Jul-2 Aug 2026; n = 600 Jews + 151 Arabs; ±3.58%.
findings.authors: Tamar Hermann; Lior Yohanani; Yaron Kaplan (Israel Democracy Institute)
findings.title: Overwhelming Majority of Israelis Think There is Danger to the Integrity of Israel's Elections (July 2026 Israeli Voice Index)
findings.relevance: The draft and equal burden is the cross-bloc wedge to use with traditional, Russian-speaking and soft-Likud voters (D5-F11, D5-F14). It should be framed as fairness to those who serve, not as hostility to Haredim (D8-F31). Lead with judicial and AG issues only for the base.

findings.topic: Arab parties in the coalition: the Netanyahu bloc's strongest wedge
findings.claim: In July 2026, most Jews opposed including Ra'am in the next government even after Mansour Abbas affirmed Israel's Jewish character. Only the strongly left and centre-left camps had majorities in favour. Maariv's poll of 7-8 October 2026 found a clear majority against an Arab party in the next coalition, but a majority for a Haredi party. A Times of Israel headline (early October, unverified) reported the Joint List as willing to give an anti-Netanyahu coalition a parliamentary 'safety net'.
findings.quant: IDI (Jews): 32.0% support Ra'am inclusion, 61.0% oppose; Arabs 27.8% support, 60.2% oppose. Maariv/Lazar (n = 700, ±3.7): Arab party in coalition 36% support, 59% oppose; Haredi party 53% support, 41% oppose. Same poll: certain to vote 86% of opposition vs 81% of coalition supporters.
findings.authors: Tamar Hermann, Lior Yohanani & Yaron Kaplan (IDI) | Moshe Cohen (The Jerusalem Post), reporting Lazar Research/Panel4All for Maariv
findings.title: July 2026 Israeli Voice Index | Coalition, opposition tie at 52 seats as Netanyahu's Likud gets closer to Eisenkot's Yashar - poll
findings.venue: Israel Democracy Institute | The Jerusalem Post
findings.relevance: Expect Likud's closing argument to be an 'Arab-backed government' message, the 2021 Bennett-Lapid-Ra'am precedent. Change-bloc messaging to Jewish swing voters should not make Arab-party cooperation salient. It should inoculate early (D8-F33) and keep a Zionist-majority frame. The model already makes Arab-sector work a leadership decision. Anti-Arab messaging carries a known backlash risk (D3-F32, D2-F24).

findings.topic: October 7 accountability among Netanyahu-bloc voters
findings.claim: Three years on, most Israelis still back a state commission of inquiry. Among coalition voters, how many back accountability depends heavily on wording and on whether Netanyahu is named. In October 2023, 69% of 2022 Likud voters said Netanyahu should publicly take responsibility. By October 2026 only 27% of coalition voters said he bears 'a great deal' of responsibility. Between 37% and 52% of coalition voters support a state commission, depending on the survey. Two in five voters say October 7 does not affect their vote at all.
findings.quant: N12 (released Mon 5 Oct 2026, reported by Maariv/JPost 6 Oct; fieldwork and n not given): Netanyahu bears 'a great deal' of responsibility 65% (opposition voters 91%, coalition 27%); state commission 66% (opposition 93%, coalition 37%, Arab-party voters 80%); October 7 affects my vote to a very great or great extent 33%, small 22%, not at all 41%. INSS (published 24 Sep 2026): state commission 75%, coalition voters 52%. Maariv/Lazar (18-19 Oct 2023, n = 510): 80% said Netanyahu should take responsibility, including 69% of Likud voters.
findings.authors: N12 poll (reported by Maariv/The Jerusalem Post) | Mora Deitch, Idit Shafran Gittleman, Abir Gitlin & Gal Shani (INSS) | Michael Bachner (Times of Israel), reporting Lazar/Panel4All for Maariv
findings.title: Nearly half of Israelis equally blame government, IDF for October 7 failures, poll finds | Special Survey: Three Years since October 7 | Poll: 80% of Israelis say Netanyahu must take public responsibility for Oct. 7 failures
findings.venue: The Jerusalem Post | INSS | The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: Netanyahu-bloc voters have re-sorted along partisan lines, consistent with D8-F11 and D8-F02. A message about Netanyahu's personal guilt reaches only about a quarter of them. A message for a state commission and for lessons for the IDF reaches roughly a third to a half. Use the institutional frame with soft-right voters and keep the personal frame for the base.

findings.topic: Trust gap: IDF vs government (INSS, Sep 2026)
findings.claim: INSS's third-anniversary survey found far more satisfaction with the IDF's conduct of the Gaza war than with the government's. A majority think an October 7-type attack could recur from Gaza. Fewer than half highly trust the IDF's own investigations. Confidence in the IDF's ability to defend Judea and Samaria communities has fallen.
findings.quant: Satisfied with IDF conduct 61% vs government 34%. Could recur from Gaza: 59% (up from 52%). High trust in IDF investigations 44% (Jews 47%). Security better than before Oct 7: 38%, worse 32%. IDF readiness to defend: south 54%, north 49%, Judea and Samaria 33% (from 39%). May 2026 INSS: high trust in IDF 74%, government 26%.
findings.authors: Mora Deitch; Idit Shafran Gittleman; Abir Gitlin; Gal Shani
findings.title: Special Survey: Three Years since October 7
findings.relevance: The 27-point gap between the IDF and the government is the space a former chief of staff can occupy: 'I trust the soldiers, I don't trust this government's judgement'. Messages should praise the army and attack government decisions, never the reverse.

findings.topic: Negative campaigning: meta-analysis
findings.claim: Pooling 111 studies through mid-2006, the authors find no reliable evidence that negative campaigning wins votes. Attacks only modestly lower feelings toward the target, and backlash against the sponsor is common. Negative messages are more memorable and slightly raise campaign knowledge. There is no reliable evidence that they depress turnout, though they slightly lower political efficacy and trust.
findings.quant: 111 studies. Net vote effect of negativity: not distinguishable from zero. Turnout: no reliable effect. Efficacy and trust: small negative.
findings.authors: Richard R. Lau; Lee Sigelman; Ivy Brown Rovner
findings.title: The Effects of Negative Political Campaigns: A Meta-Analytic Reassessment
findings.relevance: Pure attack ads on Netanyahu will not convert voters. Contrast ads that pair a specific failure with the bloc's own fix are what remain. Because negative messages are memorable, they suit high-salience accountability facts, such as the commission being blocked.

findings.topic: When negativity demobilises
findings.claim: In a lab experiment that varied only the tone of otherwise identical ads, negative ads lowered stated intention to vote, alongside lower efficacy. Later work explains why the wider literature is mixed. Negativity demobilises only when a voter sees it after having picked a preferred candidate and the attack is aimed at that candidate.
findings.quant: Ansolabehere et al.: intention to vote down 5 percentage points (lab). Krupnikov: conditional effect, 2004 campaign data and ANES 1976-2000.
findings.authors: Stephen Ansolabehere, Shanto Iyengar, Adam Simon & Nicholas Valentino | Yanna Krupnikov
findings.title: Does Attack Advertising Demobilize the Electorate? | When Does Negativity Demobilize? Tracing the Conditional Effect of Negative Campaigning on Voter Turnout
findings.venue: American Political Science Review 88(4):829-838 | American Journal of Political Science 55(4):797-813
findings.relevance: Accountability material on Netanyahu shown late to soft-Likud voters who have already chosen Likud can push some toward abstention, which is a legitimate net gain for the bloc (cf. 58% definite Likud retention, D5-F11). The same logic warns against intra-bloc attacks on Yashar or Together leaders aimed at the bloc's own decided voters.

findings.topic: Multi-candidate races: attacks help the bystander
findings.claim: A field experiment in the 2015 mayoral race in Cava de' Tirreni, Italy (incumbent plus two main challengers; canvassing randomised across 55 precincts), plus a survey experiment, studied negative ads in races with more than two candidates. A negative ad by one challenger against the incumbent did not hurt the incumbent. It produced backlash against the attacker and mainly benefited the idle third candidate. Voters saw the attacker as less cooperative, less able to lead a successful government and more extreme.
findings.quant: Idle candidate's vote share +3.7 percentage points when the incumbent was attacked by the other challenger. No effect on the target.
findings.authors: Vincenzo Galasso; Tommaso Nannicini; Salvatore Nunnari
findings.title: Positive Spillovers from Negative Campaigning
findings.relevance: In Israel's multiparty field, attacks within the bloc (Together against Yashar, D5-F18) hand votes to bystanders and make the attacker look uncooperative, the worst trait for a would-be coalition leader. Attacks on Likud are better delivered by surrogates or civil-society voices than by the list leaders whose 'can lead a government' image is at stake.

findings.topic: Out-group animosity drives online engagement
findings.claim: Across 2.7 million Facebook and Twitter posts from US news outlets and members of Congress, posts mentioning the political out-group were shared about twice as often as posts about the in-group. Out-group language was the strongest predictor of sharing, far stronger than negative or moral-emotional words, and it strongly predicted 'angry' reactions.
findings.quant: Each out-group term raised the odds of a share by 67% (OR 1.67). Angry reactions OR 2.19. About 4.8x the effect of negative-affect language and 6.7x that of moral-emotional language. n = 2,730,215 posts (observational).
findings.authors: Steve Rathje; Jay J. Van Bavel; Sander van der Linden
findings.title: Out-group animosity drives engagement on social media
findings.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(26):e2024292118
findings.relevance: Organic reach rewards content mocking Bibists, Haredim or settlers. That content is exactly what reaches and angers the other camp (D8-F24) and fuels Likud's mobilisation narrative. Judge content by the reaction it draws among persuadable and Netanyahu-bloc viewers, not by shares.

findings.topic: Emotional cues in ads: enthusiasm mobilises, fear persuades
findings.claim: In two experiments during a real 1998 Massachusetts primary, the same ad script was shown with or without emotional music and images. Enthusiasm cues raised interest and stated intention to vote and made existing preferences more stable. Fear cues did not raise turnout intention but improved recall of related news and made viewers far more open to switching to the sponsor.
findings.quant: Enthusiasm (N = 116): intention to vote +29 pp (p < .05); preference stability +16 pp. Fear (N = 118): persuasion to sponsor +26 pp (p < .001); recall of related news +21 pp; no turnout effect. Small lab samples; real-world ad effects are far smaller (P-F04, P-F05).
findings.authors: Ted Brader
findings.title: Striking a Responsive Chord: How Political Ads Motivate and Persuade Voters by Appealing to Emotions
findings.relevance: Split the creative by audience. Hopeful, enthusiastic material should go to the bloc's own supporters for turnout. Threat and loss material should go to the persuadable (soft right, traditional), where it opens re-evaluation. Do not use fear-based creative as a turnout tool.

findings.topic: Anger mobilises more than anxiety
findings.claim: Using an experiment, a national 2008 survey and pooled ANES data from 1980-2004, the authors find that anger, more than anxiety or enthusiasm, drives political participation. Anxiety prompts information-seeking. Anger prompts action.
findings.quant: Consistent across one randomised experiment, a 2008 national survey and ANES 1980-2004 (pooled).
findings.authors: Nicholas A. Valentino; Ted Brader; Eric W. Groenendyk; Krysha Gregorowicz; Vincent L. Hutchings
findings.title: Election Night's Alright for Fighting: The Role of Emotions in Political Participation
findings.relevance: For the bloc's own base, which is already more certain to vote (D8-F15, D6-F38), anger at specific failures (draft evasion, the blocked commission) is the mobilising emotion. The same anger aimed at the other side's voters mobilises them too (D8-F24), so aim it at decisions and leaders, not at groups of voters.

findings.topic: Threats to a party's status mobilise its strong identifiers
findings.claim: Across four studies, a multi-item partisan identity scale predicted campaign activity better than strong issue positions or ideology. In experiments, strong partisans became angrier when their party was threatened with electoral loss and more enthusiastic when reassured of victory. Threats to the party's status aroused more anger and enthusiasm than threatened losses on central policy issues.
findings.quant: Four studies. The emotional reactions to threat of loss or reassurance of victory are concentrated among strong identifiers. No equivalent arousal for strong issue holders.
findings.authors: Leonie Huddy; Lilliana Mason; Lene Aarøe
findings.title: Expressive Partisanship: Campaign Involvement, Political Emotion, and Partisan Identity
findings.relevance: Messages like 'Likud is finished' or 'the end of the Netanyahu era', and visible celebration of a change-bloc lead, threaten Likud identifiers' group status. That provokes the anger that mobilises them, the classic 'gevalt' dynamic, and Likud plans to exploit it with station turnout releases (D5-F27). Present the race as close and about policy failures, not as a defeat for a tribe.

findings.topic: Fear and loss appeals persuade, especially with an efficacy step
findings.claim: A meta-analysis of 127 papers finds fear appeals reliably shift attitudes, intentions and behaviours. They work better when they include efficacy statements (a clear action that removes the threat), depict high severity and susceptibility, and recommend one-time actions. No conditions were found under which they backfired. In political arguments specifically, frames that evoke loss aversion through fear were more persuasive even when a counterargument was present (Arceneaux 2012).
findings.quant: Tannenbaum et al.: 248 samples, N = 27,372, random-effects d = 0.29. Effects larger with efficacy statements and for one-off behaviours. Arceneaux: two experiments; loss-framed arguments rated stronger despite counterarguments.
findings.authors: Melanie B. Tannenbaum, Justin Hepler, Rick S. Zimmerman, Lindsey Saul, Samantha Jacobs, Kristina Wilson & Dolores Albarracín | Kevin Arceneaux
findings.title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories | Cognitive Biases and the Strength of Political Arguments
findings.venue: Psychological Bulletin 141(6):1178-1204 | American Journal of Political Science 56(2):271-285
findings.relevance: Voting is a one-time action, which suits fear appeals. Pair loss frames ('another four years without a commission or a draft law') with a concrete step: vote, and vote for a list sure to pass. That also supports threshold-rescue messaging (P-F25). Because Israeli threat perceptions push voters hawkish (D8-F11), the fear should be about mismanagement, not about the enemy.

findings.topic: Moral reframing: arguments in the target's values
findings.claim: Across six studies on issues including same-sex marriage, universal health care, military spending and English as the official language, advocates spontaneously argued from their own moral values. Arguments reframed into the opposing side's values, such as loyalty, patriotism and purity for conservatives or fairness and care for liberals, were usually more persuasive, because they increased the perceived fit between the position and the target's values. Applied to the 2016 campaign, an anti-Trump message grounded in loyalty lowered conservatives' warmth toward Trump and their likelihood of voting for him more than a fairness-grounded message. It had no effect on moderates.
findings.quant: Voelkel & Feinberg Study 1 (MTurk, N = 397, Aug 2016): conservatives' likelihood of voting for Trump (0-100) was 74.6 after the fairness argument vs 55.8 after the loyalty argument (b = -18.9, p = .004; n = 45/40). No effect for moderates (b = -0.45, n.s.).
findings.authors: Matthew Feinberg & Robb Willer | Jan G. Voelkel & Matthew Feinberg
findings.title: From Gulf to Bridge: When Do Moral Arguments Facilitate Political Influence? | Morally Reframed Arguments Can Affect Support for Political Candidates
findings.venue: Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 41(12):1665-1681 | Social Psychological and Personality Science 9(8):917-924
findings.relevance: For soft-right and traditional voters, frame the case against the government in loyalty, sanctity and authority terms rather than fairness and rights. Loyalty means betraying soldiers and reservists and abandoning hostages and the north. Sanctity means Jewish tradition's own case for sharing the burden. Authority means respect for the IDF chain and for a state commission. The rights-based case (democracy, equality) is for the base. These are online lab samples, so test before scaling (D8-F32).

findings.topic: How much moral appeals move behaviour: meta-analysis and field test
findings.claim: A 2026 meta-analysis of 67 papers (399 effects) finds moral appeals have a small positive effect on behavioural intentions and behaviour. Negative framing and including a social norm made them more effective. Assertive, controlling language made them less effective. In a preregistered field experiment, Planned Parenthood canvassers listened for each voter's moral values and tailored appeals to them. This produced large effects on interest in taking action and some evidence of attitude change (n = 1,034 voters).
findings.quant: Xu et al.: d = 0.22 (k = 399). Kalla et al.: 52 canvassers, 1,034 voters; 'large effects' on action interest; attitude effects weaker.
findings.authors: Sylvia Y. Xu, Laetitia B. Mulder, Floor A. Rink, Tammo H. A. Bijmolt & Marijke C. Leliveld | Joshua L. Kalla, Adam Seth Levine & David E. Broockman
findings.title: The Behavioral Impact of Moral Appeals: An Integrated Framework and Meta-Analysis | Personalizing Moral Reframing in Interpersonal Conversation: A Field Experiment
findings.venue: Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (online first) | The Journal of Politics 84(2):1239-1243
findings.relevance: Expect small effects (d of about 0.2) from value-framed broadcast messages. The larger payoff is in door and phone conversations where volunteers first elicit the voter's values, which fits the relational and list programmes (D3-F12). Avoid 'you must' language with Netanyahu-bloc voters.

findings.topic: Source credibility limits framing; out-party leaders polarise
findings.claim: Lab experiments show that a frame shifts opinion only when its source is seen as credible. Elites cannot reframe issues for audiences that distrust them. In 2008 survey experiments, an out-party leader's endorsement pushed partisans away from a policy, while their own leader's endorsement did not persuade them. Named politicians, more than party labels, acted as polarising cues.
findings.quant: Druckman: two lab experiments; framing effect present only with credible sources. Nicholson: in-party leader cues n.s.; out-party leader cues polarise (Obama/McCain; Bush).
findings.authors: James N. Druckman | Stephen P. Nicholson
findings.title: On the Limits of Framing Effects: Who Can Frame? | Polarizing Cues
findings.venue: The Journal of Politics 63(4):1041-1066 | American Journal of Political Science 56(1):52-66
findings.relevance: Lapid, Golan and other left-coded figures fronting a message to soft-Likud voters will push them away from it. Assign messengers by audience. Soft-right and traditional voters should hear from Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, Kahana-type religious figures and local Likud-voting notables. The base should hear from Golan and Lapid. Arceneaux & Kolodny (P-F14) show the same backlash in the field.

findings.topic: Military elite cues and 'costly' in-group critics
findings.claim: Survey experiments with nearly 12,000 US respondents found that telling people senior military leaders opposed an intervention raised public opposition. Military endorsements of support moved opinion less. The effect worked mainly through the mission's perceived legitimacy. Baum & Groeling show that criticism of a war from the president's own party, a costly signal, is more credible than criticism from the opposition, which is discounted as cheap talk.
findings.quant: Golby et al.: n of about 12,000. Opposition cues larger than support cues. Mediated mainly by perceived legitimacy, less by perceived success. Baum & Groeling: no pooled effect size stated here (abstract not retrieved).
findings.authors: James Golby, Peter Feaver & Kyle Dropp | Matthew A. Baum & Tim Groeling
findings.title: Elite Military Cues and Public Opinion About the Use of Military Force | Shot by the Messenger: Partisan Cues and Public Opinion Regarding National Security and War
findings.relevance: Former generals, Shin Bet and Mossad chiefs, and reservist commanders are most persuasive when they warn against a specific government decision (legitimacy), not when they endorse a list. Former Likud ministers, right-wing reservists and bereaved families from the right carry the 'costly signal' premium with soft-Likud voters. A 2015 public statement by about 186 retired generals and security chiefs against Netanyahu did not stop his win, so use individual, in-group voices rather than mass letters (reported precedent; no causal estimate).

findings.topic: Religious coded cues reach religious voters without alienating others
findings.claim: An experiment on the US Republican 'God talk' code, religious phrases embedded in political speech, found it was an effective cue for white evangelical Protestants. It had no effect on mainline Protestants and Catholics: it moved the in-group without costing support among others.
findings.quant: Experimental. Effect for white evangelicals; null for mainline Protestants and Catholics.
findings.authors: Brian Robert Calfano; Paul A. Djupe
findings.title: God Talk: Religious Cues and Electoral Support
findings.relevance: Traditional and moderate religious-Zionist voters (D5-F12, D5-F23) can be reached with Jewish-tradition language on equal burden, for example Numbers 32:6, 'Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?', and with rabbis and kippa-wearing officers as messengers. Secular base voters are unlikely to be put off. No Israeli test found; treat as a hypothesis to test.

findings.topic: Affective polarisation and what reduces it
findings.claim: Partisan hostility is now as automatic as racial bias and drives discrimination against opposing partisans (US evidence). A megastudy of 25 interventions found many reduced partisan animosity. The strongest highlighted relatable, sympathetic people with different politics, or emphasised identities shared by rivals. Correcting misperceptions of the other side and highlighting the threat of democratic collapse reduced support for undemocratic practices.
findings.quant: Iyengar & Westwood: implicit, explicit and behavioural measures; partisan discrimination exceeds racial discrimination. Voelkel et al.: n = 32,059, 25 treatments; common-identity and sympathetic-outpartisan treatments strongest on animosity.
findings.authors: Shanto Iyengar & Sean J. Westwood | Jan G. Voelkel, Michael N. Stagnaro, James Y. Chu et al.
findings.title: Fear and Loathing across Party Lines: New Evidence on Group Polarization | Megastudy testing 25 treatments to reduce antidemocratic attitudes and partisan animosity
findings.venue: American Journal of Political Science 59(3):690-707 | Science 386(6719):eadh4764
findings.relevance: Israeli affective polarisation is above US levels and rises with electoral competition (D1-F04, P-F15). Undecided Jews want unity (D5-F22). Messages to the soft right should show sympathetic Likud voters who served, plus shared identity ('reservists from all camps'). Eisenkot's unity framing fits this. Anything that reads as contempt for Likud voters will mobilise them.

findings.topic: Message testing: targeting, format and frame strength
findings.claim: Combining message pretests with machine learning to choose which ad each person sees beat the alternative strategies by about 70% on one of two issues. Targeting on more than one trait added nothing, and the gain was smaller when choosing which attitude to target. Video makes people more likely to believe an event happened than text does, but adds little persuasion over text (n = 7,609, 72 clips). In framing experiments, how strong a frame is matters more than how often it is repeated. Competing frames reduce framing effects but do not eliminate them (Chong & Druckman).
findings.quant: Tappin et al.: microtargeting advantage of about 70% or more (Study 1), no gain beyond one covariate. Wittenberg et al.: video-vs-text persuasion gap comparable to or smaller than the text-vs-control gap. See P-F05: ads vary about ±50% around the mean.
findings.authors: Ben M. Tappin, Chloe Wittenberg, Luke B. Hewitt, Adam J. Berinsky & David G. Rand | Chloe Wittenberg, Ben M. Tappin, Adam J. Berinsky & David G. Rand | Dennis Chong & James N. Druckman
findings.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting | The (minimal) persuasive advantage of political video over text | Framing Public Opinion in Competitive Democracies
findings.venue: PNAS 120(25):e2216261120 | PNAS 118(47):e2114388118 | American Political Science Review 101(4):637-655
findings.relevance: With 14 days left, run one fast online test this week (8-12 messages, about 2,000-3,000 Jewish respondents, with soft-Netanyahu-bloc and traditional quotas). Then target by a single trait, religiosity or 2022 vote, rather than building complex segments. Cheap text and static creative is close to as persuasive as video. Pick the strongest frame and stop rotating many weak ones.

findings.topic: Inoculation against expected attacks
findings.claim: A meta-analysis of 54 cases found that inoculation messages (warning of a coming attack and refuting it in advance) conferred more resistance to persuasion than supportive messages or no treatment. Refuting the exact coming argument and refuting a different one worked about equally well. Resistance held from immediate to moderate delays but decayed after about two weeks. Inoculation was first applied to political campaigns by Pfau & Burgoon (1988).
findings.quant: 54 cases. Inoculation > supportive messages > no treatment. Resistance decays after about 14 days.
findings.authors: John A. Banas; Stephen A. Rains
findings.title: A Meta-Analysis of Research on Inoculation Theory
findings.relevance: Likud's predictable closing attacks are 'a government dependent on Arab parties' (D8-F15), 'the left' and 'reservists' refusal'. They should be pre-empted now, at D-14, and refreshed after the final polls on 23 Oct, because protection fades within about two weeks. A typical form: 'They will tell you X. The truth is Y.'

findings.topic: Turnout framing: 'everyone is voting' beats 'gevalt'; wording tricks do not scale
findings.claim: In two get-out-the-vote phone experiments (2005 New Jersey and 2006 California gubernatorial elections), messages stressing high expected turnout raised voting intention more than messages stressing low turnout. The effect was concentrated among occasional voters. A celebrated wording trick ('be a voter' instead of 'vote') raised turnout in small studies (Bryan et al. 2011), but a large field replication found no effect. It was weaker than a standard GOTV message.
findings.quant: Gerber & Rogers: certain to vote 76.3% (high-turnout script) vs 69% (low-turnout script), about +7 pp in stated intention. The figure is from a secondary summary (The Decision Lab); the paper reports the direction and the occasional-voter concentration. Gerber et al. 2016: 'noun' framing has no effect on validated turnout.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber & Todd Rogers | Christopher J. Bryan, Gregory M. Walton, Todd Rogers & Carol S. Dweck | Alan S. Gerber, Gregory A. Huber, Daniel R. Biggers & David J. Hendry
findings.title: Descriptive Social Norms and Motivation to Vote: Everybody's Voting and So Should You | Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self | A field experiment shows that subtle linguistic cues might not affect voter behavior
findings.relevance: On election day, when the station turnout releases come out (D5-F26), the bloc's mobilisation messages to its low-propensity supporters should say 'people like you are voting in record numbers', not 'turnout in Tel Aviv is collapsing'. Public 'gevalt' alarms also feed Likud's counter-mobilisation (D8-F24). Spend on contact, not on clever wording. Social-pressure details are in D3-F05.

findings.topic: Poll momentum and bandwagon
findings.claim: In a large national survey experiment in Denmark's multiparty system, news stories describing a party's poll rise or fall moved voting intentions in the same direction. Effects were strongest for rising parties and appeared for both a small and a large party. They did not vary across demographic groups.
findings.quant: National survey experiment. Bandwagon effect strongest in the positive direction. Consistent across two parties.
findings.authors: Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper M. Hansen; Martin V. Larsen
findings.title: How Election Polls Shape Voting Behaviour
findings.relevance: The final published polls on Fri 23 Oct set the momentum story for the four-day blackout. If change-bloc lists are rising, amplify it. If Yashar or the bloc is slipping (Kan, 11 Oct), avoid 'collapse' coverage and frame it as a close race (D8-F24). Pair this with threshold insurance messaging for allies near 4 seats (P-F25, P-F26).

open_questions: The shared web-search budget ran out during this desk. Not searched: defector or 'former supporter' testimonial experiments, Israeli religious-messenger effects, Channel 13 and Kan issue-ownership questions, and Russian-language or Druze message polling.

No 2026 poll found asks which leader or party is best on security, cost of living and the draft (an issue-ownership question). D8-F06 implies the security play pays only where Eisenkot is within reach of Netanyahu, so commission or locate one urgently.

No Israeli experiment found on moral reframing, ex-security messengers or religious-language cues among soft-Likud and traditional voters. All messenger recommendations are extrapolated from US and European studies; a rapid online test (D8-F32) should validate them before the 23 Oct final polls.
IDI's July 2026 camp-level figures for the draft-arrest freeze and Ra'am inclusion appear only in charts. Coalition-voter and Likud-voter breakdowns would sharpen the draft wedge estimate.
Coalition voters' support for a state commission differs by survey (N12 37% vs INSS 52%). The difference in question wording should be resolved before the bloc builds its closing message on it.

Kan (11 Oct) shows the change bloc slipping two seats in a week and Amcha crossing the threshold. No source found explains why (security events, the Arab-party safety-net story, intra-bloc fighting). This matters for whether the agenda is moving toward Likud-owned issues.
How Netanyahu-bloc voters react to the Joint List's reported 'safety net' offer, and whether pre-emptive inoculation (D8-F33) reduces it, is untested.

Is there a measurable counter-mobilisation effect from Likud's planned use of station turnout releases (D5-F27)? If so, the bloc's own public turnout messaging on election day should be quieter than its private contact programme.
